meta.title: Who really said "We must reach out our hand in friendship both to those who would befriend us and those who would be our enemy"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, Arthur Ashe wrote it — in Days of Grace (1993), p. 186. The version everyone shares adds two words he did not write: “and dignity”.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We must reach out our hand in friendship both to those who would befriend us and those who would be our enemy'?
meta.ogDescription: Arthur Ashe really wrote this, in his 1993 memoir Days of Grace. The popular quote-card version inserts “and dignity”, which the sourced text does not contain.

answer.sourceLine: The sentence is from Days of Grace: A Memoir, the book Ashe wrote with Arnold Rampersad and finished, according to Wikipedia’s account of his final months ↗, less than a week before he died in February 1993. Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ transcribes the line inside its full paragraph and places it at p. 186 — though the widely shared card version adds two words, “and dignity,” that the sourced text does not have.

source.excerpt: … We must reach out our hand in friendship both to those who would befriend us and those who would be our enemy. We must believe in the power of education. …
trail: Wikiquote’s Arthur Ashe page ↗ carries the line in a sourced section headed “Days of Grace: A Memoir (1994)”, quoting the whole paragraph and citing p. 186 — wording that matches the quote under investigation exactly, with no “and dignity”.

The book itself checks out: Open Library’s edition record ↗ gives Days of Grace: A Memoir, Alfred A. Knopf, 1993, 317 pages, “by Arthur Ashe and Arnold Rampersad”, and the Internet Archive copy ↗ is a scan of that first edition.

The 1994 edition Wikiquote cites is longer than the 317-page hardcover — Open Library records the 1994 Ballantine paperback at 352 pages — which is why its page references (p. 186 here, p. 341 for Ashe’s message to his daughter Camera) run past the first edition’s length. We did not inspect the page itself; the page number is Wikiquote’s, and AZQuotes ↗ gives the same page for the same paragraph.

Quote Investigator ↗ has examined a different Ashe line (“True heroism is remarkably sober…”, which it credits to his 1991 Ohio Wesleyan University commencement address) but has no article on this sentence, and we found no source crediting it to anyone other than Ashe.
source.excerptNote: The sentence is not free-standing advice about making friends. It sits inside a paragraph in which Ashe argues that the growing isolation of Black America — however much it reads as pride and self-affirmation — is not the answer to its problems, and which closes with him saying he sees no conflict between being proud of one’s ancestors and seeing oneself first as a member of a commonwealth of all races and creeds. The full paragraph is transcribed at Wikiquote ↗.

author.name: Arthur Ashe
author.heading: Arthur Ashe
author.metaLine: 1943–1993 · American tennis champion, author and activist
author.bio: Arthur Ashe was born in Richmond, Virginia in 1943 and became the only Black man ever to win the singles title at Wimbledon, the US Open and the Australian Open. Off the court he was an organiser and an arguer — captain of the US Davis Cup team from 1981 to 1985, arrested outside the South African embassy in Washington in January 1985 at an anti-apartheid rally, and, after announcing in April 1992 that a blood transfusion had left him HIV-positive, one of the most prominent AIDS campaigners in the country. He wrote Days of Grace with Arnold Rampersad in his last months, finishing the manuscript less than a week before his death on 6 February 1993; that June he was posthumously awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: Nobody has stolen this line from Arthur Ashe, and nobody has pinned it on him falsely — the authorship is sound. What has happened is smaller and sneakier: the sentence has been edited on its way around the internet, and severed from the argument it was making.

items.why: The most-shared form runs “We must reach out our hand in friendship and dignity both to those who would befriend us…” — and it travels without a page reference; Lib Quotes ↗ carries it that way. Tellingly, AZQuotes ↗ hosts both: an unsourced standalone entry with “and dignity”, and a longer entry sourced to Days of Grace, p. 186, which reads simply “in friendship”.

Detached from its paragraph the line reads as generic advice about being nice to difficult people. In the book it is one clause of a public argument: the paragraph Wikiquote transcribes ↗ is Ashe rejecting racial isolation as an answer to Black America’s problems, ending with his insistence that pride in one’s ancestors and membership in a commonwealth of all races are not in conflict.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is genuinely Arthur Ashe’s, from Days of Grace — sourced at p. 186 ↗. If you quote it, quote it without “and dignity”, and remember it was written about a country, not about a friendship.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Ashe wrote Days of Grace against a clock. He had announced in April 1992 that a transfusion during 1980s heart surgery had left him HIV-positive; he finished the manuscript less than a week before he died on 6 February 1993, and Alfred A. Knopf published it that year. A book written under those conditions tends to say what its author actually thinks, and this passage is one of the places where he does.

The sentence is not a pleasantry. It sits in a paragraph where Ashe argues against the pull toward racial isolation — conceding that it can look like pride and self-affirmation, and answering that it is still not the answer. Reaching a hand to “those who would be our enemy” is the practical edge of that argument, not a general rule about being gracious.
context.detailsSummary: More on the book, and a note on the page number
detailsBody: The memoir’s chapter list, recorded in the Internet Archive’s catalogue entry for the Knopf first edition ↗, shows how much ground it covers: “My outing”, “Middle passage”, “Stars and stripes: a captain in the Davis Cup wars”, “Protest and politics”, “The burden of race”, “The striving and achieving”, “The beast in the jungle”, “Sex and sports in the age of AIDS”, “Stepping up”, “The threads in my hands” and “My dear Camera”. That last chapter is the farewell letter to his daughter which supplies the book’s other most-quoted passages.

A note on the page number: Wikiquote cites p. 186 of the 1994 edition, which is the longer paperback — Open Library records it at 352 pages against the 1993 hardcover’s 317 — so its pagination does not map onto the first edition. We have not inspected the page itself; the citation is Wikiquote’s, and AZQuotes gives the same page for the same paragraph.
context.pull: It is an argument about isolation, not a greeting card about friendship.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced section for Arthur Ashe, headed "Days of Grace: A Memoir (1994)", transcribes the paragraph containing "We must reach out our hand in friendship both to those who would befriend us and those who would be our enemy. We must believe in the power of education." and cites p. 186. It gives Ashe's dates as 10 July 1943 - 6 February 1993 and cites his message to his daughter Camera at p. 341.

Open Library edition record OL1745462M gives Days of Grace: A Memoir, Alfred A. Knopf / Distributed by Random House, 1993, 317 pages, ISBN 0679423966, "by Arthur Ashe and Arnold Rampersad". Open Library also records the Ballantine Books 1994 edition (ISBN 0345386817) at 352 pages.

The Internet Archive item daysofgracememoi00ashe is a scan of Days of Grace: A Memoir, New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 1993, and its catalogue record lists the chapters: My outing; Middle passage; Stars and stripes: a captain in the Davis Cup wars; Protest and politics; The burden of race; The striving and achieving; The beast in the jungle; Sex and sports in the age of AIDS; Stepping up; The threads in my hands; My dear Camera.

Wikipedia states Ashe was born 10 July 1943 in Richmond, Virginia and died 6 February 1993 in New York City; that he is the only Black man to win the singles titles at Wimbledon, the US Open and the Australian Open; that he captained the US Davis Cup team from 1981 to 1985; that he was arrested on 11 January 1985 protesting outside the South African embassy in Washington; that he publicly announced on 8 April 1992 that he had contracted HIV; that he finished the Days of Grace manuscript less than a week before his death; and that he was posthumously awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom on 20 June 1993.

Quote Investigator credits Arthur Ashe with "True heroism is remarkably sober, very undramatic...", tracing it to his commencement address at Ohio Wesleyan University on 12 May 1991. The article does not mention Days of Grace or the phrase "reach out our hand in friendship".

Lib Quotes carries the variant wording "We must reach out our hand in friendship and dignity both to those who would befriend us and those who would be our enemy", credited to Days of Grace: A Memoir, with no page number.

AZQuotes' Arthur Ashe page carries both an unsourced standalone version reading "in friendship and dignity" and a longer version sourced to Days of Grace: A Memoir by Arthur Ashe and Arnold Rampersad, p. 186, which includes the surrounding context about isolation and spiritual values.
